item.title: Japan’s popular prime minister is burning political capital fast
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Takaichi’s travails STANDING BEFORE an elaborate array of white flowers, Takaichi Sanae, Japan’s prime minister, delivered a speech at a memorial this month in honour of Abe Shinzo, a former prime minister assassinated four years ago. Ms Takaichi, who positions herself as Abe’s political...
item.content:encoded:
Japan’s popular prime minister is burning political capital fast

Asia | Takaichi’s travails


STANDING BEFORE an elaborate array of white flowers, Takaichi Sanae, Japan’s prime minister, delivered a speech at a memorial this month in honour of Abe Shinzo, a former prime minister assassinated four years ago. Ms Takaichi, who positions herself as Abe’s political heir, praised her mentor’s fortitude. “I want to be a politician who fights like Mr Abe,” she said.

And fight she must. In February Ms Takaichi led her ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to a historic victory in the election to the powerful lower house of the Diet, amassing a two-thirds supermajority. Despite this she has struggled to enact her hawkish, big-spending, socially conservative agenda. The LDP and its allies had to extend the latest Diet session by one week, until July 25th, in order to finish their legislative business; the honebuto, an annual budget framework, was finalised only on July 21st, much later than expected. Opinion polls show the Takaichi administration’s once-stellar approval ratings falling sharply (see chart). “She’s powerful, but not all-powerful,” says Tobias Harris of Japan Foresight, a consultancy.

During the Diet session after the election, Ms Takaichi advanced on several fronts. She has made the most progress in her pledge to strengthen Japan’s defences, in both hard security and economic security. Reforms to create a new investment-screening body, modelled on CFIUS, America’s equivalent committee, sailed through parliament; the Japan Foreign Investment Committee was launched last month. The Diet also passed a bill to reform Japan’s fragmented, underwhelming intelligence capabilities and create a more powerful centralised intelligence apparatus for the first time since 1945. The first new bodies, an intelligence bureau and a council, will be established this month.

Ms Takaichi has stoked Japan’s culture wars. The LDP and its coalition partners pushed through two controversial bills favoured by social conservatives. One criminalised desecration of the Japanese flag. The most fraught concerned imperial succession. With few male heirs, the very survival of the Japanese imperial house is at risk. A vast majority of the public supports female succession, which would mean the current emperor’s only child, a daughter named Aiko, could succeed her father. Ms Takaichi promised to find a national consensus. Instead, the LDP used its supermajority to pass a bill that allows distant male relatives to succeed, while keeping women off the throne.

The prime minister also rode roughshod over her opponents on economic policy. Her first honebuto and an associated growth strategy herald a massive industrial-policy push. The new growth strategy sets a target of ¥370trn ($2.3trn) in combined public and private investment between now and 2041. The government will have a hand in stimulating 17 sectors, ranging from AI to anime, across 62 specific product areas. To do so, Ms Takaichi has introduced a new multi-year budgeting framework; she also shifted the government’s fiscal benchmark from a long-held target of achieving a budget surplus before interest payments to aiming instead for a downward trajectory in the debt-to-GDP ratio. She has continued to promise a consumption-tax cut, though implementing it has been delayed. The moves amount to a loosening of fiscal discipline, without a clear plan for how to finance the outlays.

Resistance to the prime minister has in turn been mounting from several quarters. Markets have pushed back on her big-spending plans. After the government released a draft of the honebuto last month, yields on ten-year government bonds soared to their highest levels in three decades; analysts dubbed it the “honebuto shock”. (Ms Takaichi and her allies claim the bond movements had nothing to do with their profligate plans.) When the final version of the honebuto was approved on July 21st, language underlining Bank of Japan (BoJ) independence had been added. Nonetheless, the yen weakened to its lowest level in four decades the next day, in part because of the perception that the BoJ would be loth to raise rates in the face of government pressure. Investors’ concerns about Japanese economic policy “stem from a more general sense of uncertainty surrounding the potential scale of future government spending expansion,” Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities, an investment bank, reports in a recent research note.

Grievances are also accumulating within the prime minister’s own coalition. Fiscal policy has long been an important dividing line inside the big-tent LDP. “We’re supposed to be conservative but we sound like socialists,” gripes one fiscally hawkish LDP bigwig. One heavyweight on the LDP’s consumption-tax commission resigned in protest at Ms Takaichi’s planned cuts. More socially liberal members of the party raised objections to the flag-desecration law; a former foreign minister conspicuously skipped the vote. The LDP’s new coalition partner, Ishin, has also been forced to forgo some of its priorities, such as cutting the number of seats in the Diet. Yoshimura Hirofumi, the party leader, described the outcome as “heartbreaking”.

Most crucially, Ms Takaichi’s domineering style has helped unite a fractious and ideologically diverse group of opposition parties against her. “The opposition came together and said we don’t agree on policy, but we do agree that the LDP has overstepped,” says Nishimura Rintaro of The Asia Group, a firm that gives advice on strategy. In the upper house, where the ruling coalition is a few seats shy of a majority, the remaining parties banded together to halt Diet proceedings in late June. In theory, the LDP can override the upper house with its lower-house supermajority. But in practice doing so would come with significant political costs. As a result, Ms Takaichi has passed bills at a slower rate than any of the three most recent prime ministers; even her immediate predecessor, Ishiba Shigeru, who led a minority government in both houses, had more legislation quickly approved.

The messy management of the Diet mirrors broader complaints about Ms Takaichi’s leadership style. In a culture that stresses consensus, Ms Takaichi has disdained the schmoozing that traditionally helps build it. She prefers to communicate with the public through social media, eschewing press conferences or formal interviews. Business leaders gripe that she does not consult them. The prime minister is “a loner”, says one Japanese chief executive. Bureaucrats also lament that she does not listen to them. She would rather read briefing papers than have “real discussions with advisers”, says a senior official. Ms Takaichi boasts about studying so hard that she sleeps no more than three hours a night.

The qualities that have alienated power-brokers still appeal to voters. Her plain-spoken style, everywoman background and punishing work ethic made her one of the most popular prime ministers in modern Japanese history, with approval ratings around 70% following her big election win.

But that popularity, the foundation of Ms Takaichi’s power, is starting to erode. Voter frustration with persistent inflation, and a backlash against the imperial-succession law, have helped drive approval ratings for Ms Takaichi’s administration down steadily. With more than a year until the next party-leadership election, Ms Takaichi is hardly in danger of losing power. But her heavy-handed approach ensures that more fights will follow. ■

item.title: The Chinese economic experiment that failed
item.description:
China

China | Bottom of the class From the late 1970s, as China moved away from central planning, the Communist Party picked four cities on the coast to be test-beds for liberal economic policies. Known as “special economic zones” (sez), three of them, Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Xiamen, have been world-ch...
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese economic experiment that failed

China | Bottom of the class


From the late 1970s, as China moved away from central planning, the Communist Party picked four cities on the coast to be test-beds for liberal economic policies. Known as “special economic zones” (sez), three of them, Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Xiamen, have been world-changing successes, showing the way for market reforms in the rest of the country. The other one is Shantou.

You rarely hear about Shantou. The city of 5.6m was one of China’s first trading ports, and is the hometown of economic heroes such as Li Ka-shing, Hong Kong’s richest man, and Pony Ma, founder of Tencent, a tech giant. Yet it is not thriving. Last year its gdp per person was 54,000 yuan ($8,000), comparable to Gansu, China’s poorest province in the far west, and well below the national average of 100,000 yuan (never mind Shenzhen’s 214,000 yuan). Locals refer to it as a “special economically backward zone”. Growth was just 0.1% last year. So why did three cities flourish from special treatment, while one floundered?

Shantou’s gdp in 1980 was four times that of Shenzhen, where gdp is now ten times Shantou’s. But it had some disadvantages. Initially, just 1.6 square kilometres was carved out for its sez, the smallest of all four cities. Its location is awkward. Shenzhen is next to Hong Kong, Zhuhai next to Macau, and Xiamen across the strait from Taiwan. Shantou is relatively isolated on Guangdong province’s east coast. Yet by 1991, its sez had expanded to cover all 234 square kilometres of its landmass. And plenty of cities inland have outpaced Shantou despite being more remote (besides, high-speed rail now connects up all such major metropolises).

What went so wrong? The property downturn has hit Shantou harder than many other places. Fixed-asset investment in property fell by a staggering 38.8% last year. Consumption is sputtering along. In a cluster of three malls in the city centre, two stand largely deserted. So do many restaurants. And the city’s industry is weak. While places like Shenzhen moved up the value chain, Shantou bred local champions in toymaking and textiles, low-margin and labour-intensive industries that made up nearly half the city’s big firms in 2024. They are struggling too. In 2025 exports of toys fell by 8.6% and garments by 18.3%. Exports dipped by 9.1% overall, puzzling for a port city (in a year when China racked up a record $1.2trn trade surplus).

To understand Shantou’s deeper troubles, look to culture and institutions. Locals speak of unusually egregious corruption in the city. One retired businessman recounts how, at the start of every year, city officials would turn up to pester him for bribes, threatening to cause trouble if he didn’t pay up. Visits to hospital can require a cash bribe to the doctor. The rot goes so deep that in 2000 graft-busters sent to Shantou from the central government were killed in a large hotel blaze—a suspected arson attack. Corruption remains an issue for many in the city.

A more unusual problem is mistrust of outsiders. China has long viewed foreigners with suspicion, but locals in Shantou regard even Chinese people not from the city as outsiders (referring to them as “out-of-province kids”). A big source of this is the local dialect which, owing to the city’s historic isolation, is unintelligible to Mandarin speakers in the rest of the country. People not from Shantou find it difficult to integrate there. One doctor who now lives abroad recalls how colleagues discriminated against him at the city’s central hospital for being from Zhejiang province.

All this has helped to keep businesses, talent and investment away. Between 1996 and 2017 Shantou received just $6.7bn in foreign direct investment (fdi), compared with Shenzhen’s $85bn, according to research by Lang Liu and Michael Plouffe of University College London. More troubling, fdi has been negatively correlated with gdp (see chart), meaning that as the economy grew, outside investment actually shrank. Talented youngsters leave and do not return. Overall the city’s poor reputation seems to discourage people from moving there for work.

There is one bright spot, at least. In 2025 the number of overnight visitors rose by 12.8%, and revenue from tourism grew by 23.9%, enough to keep recession at bay. Local authorities have restored the old town, once a dilapidated district of crumbling colonial-era buildings, and turned it into a tourist hotspot. Now the area is buzzing with visitors at night. A souvenir seller says that the recent hit film “Dear You”, which was partly shot there, has increased footfall.

Shantou’s story is a case study of what happens when top-down directives meet local constraints. Policy support can supercharge growth if the right conditions already exist locally, but cannot create them. China’s policymakers would do well to take heed, as they try to fulfil their vision of a high-tech future across the country. As for Shantou, it was meant to usher in reform across China. Ironically, it is better known for preserving its past than for shaping the country’s future. ■

Subscribers can sign up to Drum Tower, our new weekly newsletter, to understand what the world makes of China—and what China makes of the world.

item.title: China’s shadowy maritime militia is worryingly active
item.description:
China

China | The third fleet THE BAYS OF the Zhoushan archipelago are crammed with blue-hulled fishing boats, laid up after a busy season scouring the East China Sea for crabs and croaker. Some of the boats, though, have been doing more than just fishing. In December over 1,000 vessels from Zhoushan...
item.content:encoded:
China’s shadowy maritime militia is worryingly active

China | The third fleet


THE BAYS OF the Zhoushan archipelago are crammed with blue-hulled fishing boats, laid up after a busy season scouring the East China Sea for crabs and croaker. Some of the boats, though, have been doing more than just fishing. In December over 1,000 vessels from Zhoushan and other parts of China’s eastern seaboard did something unprecedented. They lined up in an inverted L-shape in the seas north of Taiwan, held the formation for more than 12 hours, then dispersed (see maps). Over the next few months Chinese fishing boats coalesced again in the East China Sea, on four more occasions.

Chinese state-run media claim all this is normal commercial activity. Something fishier is surely going on. China is unusual in having three separate maritime forces at its disposal. The first two are the navy and the coastguard. But since as far back as the 1950s, China’s leaders have also commandeered part of the country’s fishing fleet as a paramilitary “maritime militia”. This shadowy force is made up of a mixture of normal fishing boats and larger, steel-hulled ones which appear to be purpose-built for aggressive manoeuvres. It is notorious for its activities in the South China Sea, where militia boats are often sent to disputed reefs and islets to press China’s sovereignty claims, sometimes violently.

Fishing boats in the East China Sea had largely stuck to trawling. That may be changing. The recent formations there were far larger than anything seen before, even in the South China Sea, so it seems likely that they brought together many ordinary fishing vessels alongside formal militiamen. They were packed densely enough that some cargo ships appeared to change course to go around them. The manoeuvres suggest that Chinese officials are testing out their capabilities—and some fear it could all give China an edge in a conflict over Taiwan.

No official numbers are published on the size of China’s maritime militia. State news outlets sometimes deny that it even exists. But an article published in 2014 in a Chinese defence journal praised the force as “irreplaceable” thanks to its “wide distribution, disguised identities and familiarity with maritime conditions”. Unlike its navy, China’s militia gives officials plausible deniability for ambiguous “grey zone” activities: they can claim, for instance, that violent confrontations with other countries’ ships were caused by “patriotic fishermen” acting independently.

For decades the maritime militia had a reputation as a ragtag bunch, with antiquated weapons and poor discipline. The average fisherman has only a limited education and greying hair (only 5% are below the age of 30, according to a survey in 2024; fishing is tough and few Chinese youths want to do it). That means training them to use the latest communications technologies can be a challenge. Motivation can also be a problem because compensation is reportedly low. That is partly because the militia are meant to act out of patriotic duty rather than for personal gain, says Collin Koh of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Local governments and military authorities also sometimes squabble over who should pay.

Since Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, China has been trying to build what it calls a “new style” maritime militia—one that is better equipped, trained and organised. How much is being spent on this militia is unclear. Provinces and cities contribute towards a variety of schemes, and state-owned firms are encouraged to chip in. Some fishing boats can get daily subsidies of over 24,000 yuan ($3,500) to loiter in disputed areas, more than enough to cover their costs and allow owners to profit without doing any fishing.

Modernisation has gone furthest in the South China Sea, a vast body of water which China claims almost in its entirety (six other countries, including Vietnam and the Philippines, have competing claims over the region, which is rich in fish and energy resources). Some locals have become full-time militiamen, crewing large steel-hulled vessels equipped with big water cannons. They swarm around the shoals and reefs that China claims while surveilling and harassing foreign vessels.

Militia activities are inherently hard to track, but appear to have been steadily increasing in the South China Sea. The Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, a programme at CSIS, an American think-tank, uses satellite images to check for telltale signs such as vessels loitering without deploying fishing gear, or tying themselves together to form a floating barrier. Last year it counted an average of 241 Chinese vessels that it believes were militia sailing in disputed areas of the region every day. That was the highest number since CSIS started monitoring in 2021.

China has disputes in the East China Sea too, with Japan and South Korea in addition to Taiwan. But militiamen have tended to be less aggressive in the region, instead focusing on civilian matters like emergency relief after typhoons. The East China Sea is less than one quarter of the size of the South China Sea, and China’s claims there are over specific areas such as the uninhabited Senkaku islands (known as the Diaoyu in Chinese, and which Japan controls) rather than over the entire body of water. Its coastguard should, therefore, be able to patrol and handle confrontations with other countries’ vessels without relying on civilian boats.

All of this adds to the mystery surrounding the recent formations. Five took place in less than six months, according to IngeniSPACE, a research company tracking their movements. The first assembled over 1,000 ships into two parallel arrangements, stretching 450km, around Christmas Day. During the next formation, in January, some boats stayed in place for over 30 hours. Days earlier China had conducted large-scale war games around Taiwan. In late March a new formation appeared 100km to the east and closer to Jeju, a South Korean island. Boats congregated for the latest formation, in April, on the same meridian, shortly before the start of China’s annual summer fishing ban.

Co-ordinating so many ships to stay in place for so long is a technical challenge, but more importantly a political one, says Gregory Poling of CSIS. Some countries struggle to make their fishermen broadcast their locations consistently (many prefer to keep their choicest fishing grounds a secret). China has shown “a degree of political control that no other country on earth can claim” over its civilian fleet, he notes.

What could such control be used for? In a conflict over Taiwan, the militia might help the navy with reconnaissance or logistics. Militia boats have also been accused of cutting undersea-communications cables. If China launched an amphibious invasion of Taiwan, a callous commander might use swarms of fishing boats to overwhelm the enemy with potential targets. A very large number of such vessels could play a more important role if China tried to impose a full blockade of the island, or a more calibrated “quarantine” (blocking only some goods). They could help disrupt the flow of shipping to and from its ports.

The fishermen of Zhoushan, at least, have no love lost with Taiwan. In 1950 Zhoushan was one of the last regions of China held by the Kuomintang after its defeat by the Communist Party. Thousands of local men were press-ganged to replenish its army, and forced to go to Taiwan. Some locals are still bitter. More prosaically, one grizzled captain says a conflict would be a disaster for business. He would help only if the authorities demanded it. One younger man, though, is confident that local fishermen would play their part. “We Chinese are like scattered sand that would unite if the time came,” he says. “We’d all become militia.” ■

Subscribers can sign up to Drum Tower, our new weekly newsletter, to understand what the world makes of China—and what China makes of the world.

item.title: Why criticism of the Qing dynasty scares the Communist Party
item.description:
China

China | Chaguan Visitors to historic sites around China see not only palaces and pagodas, but also scores of men and women in period dress posing for photos. To the uninitiated, one flowing robe looks like any other. But for some donning the historical threads, they are a display with political...
item.content:encoded:
Why criticism of the Qing dynasty scares the Communist Party

China | Chaguan


Visitors to historic sites around China see not only palaces and pagodas, but also scores of men and women in period dress posing for photos. To the uninitiated, one flowing robe looks like any other. But for some donning the historical threads, they are a display with political undertones: a celebration of Han traditions and a rejection of the “foreign” Qing, China’s last imperial dynasty, whose final emperor abdicated in 1912. It is a view that has gained currency, to the alarm of the Communist Party.

On a recent stroll around the Forbidden City, once the emperor’s home in the centre of Beijing, Chaguan quickly found people with these sartorial sensibilities. “Before, we might have worn Qing clothing. We’re more historically aware now. The Qing were barbarians,” says one woman, a university student in a billowing light-green dress, alongside her boyfriend in a subdued scholarly robe. Not all opting for pre-Qing clothing care much about the politics. “It’s just more refined and aesthetic,” says Ms Xu, a visitor from Fujian province, explaining her choice of an off-white Ming-style noblewoman’s outfit rather than flashier Qing garb.

Clothing is the most superficial part of the anti-Qing thinking now growing more prevalent. Discourse about the dynasty and its misdeeds has long featured in online forums, summarised as the “1644 historical view”, referring to the year that the Qing overthrew the Ming. (The Ming rulers were Han, China’s dominant ethnic group, whereas the Qing were Manchus, a smaller minority group from the north.) Social media have helped the 1644 view spread to more mainstream audiences.

In China’s official narrative, the country suffered a “century of humiliation” of foreign invasions, starting with the first opium war in 1840 and ending only with Mao’s rise to power in 1949. But the 1644 view—cheekily expressed by some online as “three centuries of humiliation”—argues that subjugation began with the Qing. According to this school, the Qing were anti-Han interlopers and, making matters worse, feckless in repelling foreign forces.

Dredging up all this history is uncomfortable for the party. The territorial boundaries claimed by modern China—including Tibet, Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia and Taiwan—were brought into the Chinese empire by the Qing, not the Ming. Grievances about the Manchus also cut against the ideal of ethnic harmony advanced by the party. Although much of what forms modern Chinese identity is derived from Han traditions, it is unseemly to talk openly about the dominance of this one ethnic group, which accounts for 90% of the Chinese population. The party looks askance at “Han chauvinism”, believing, with reason, that it may lead to more resentment from non-Han groups.

Late last year, the communications arm of the Zhejiang provincial government—known for strong opinion pieces—became the first official body to wade into the discussion. It formally condemned the 1644 view, labelling it a harmful distortion. Too much blame, it argued, was placed on the Qing for China’s troubles: the Ming had also been plagued by economic and social problems. The Zhejiang authorities warned that it was an opening for hostile Westerners to push the “new Qing history”, which emphasises the unique Manchu identity of Qing rulers.

That appears to have been the opening shot in an official rectification campaign. Since then, censors have deleted social-media accounts critical of the Qing and scrubbed many such videos and comments. In recent days the censors have been busy again. A forthcoming film, “The Belief”, is intended as a nationalist tribute to the naval expedition in 1683 that facilitated the Qing’s annexation of Taiwan. But many online have been more sympathetic towards the conquered—Han loyalists of the Ming dynasty based in Taiwan—than to the Qing soldiers sent to subdue them. In fact the 1644 view is far from novel. An early proponent of something like it was Sun Yat-sen, celebrated as a father of modern China. A leading voice for the Qing’s overthrow at the turn of the 20th century, he railed against the Manchus as outsiders.

Sensitivity over how to interpret all this illustrates how hard it is for the party to examine its own history. Never mind serious debates about Mao’s rule; even century-old dynasties are too hot to touch. The party commissioned an official history of the Qing and was close to completing it as a mammoth 106-volume project. But now it seems to have been scuppered by leaders because of disagreements about “new Qing” contamination. “It is very clear that the state was ruled by people who were not identical to the bulk of the population, so it’s hard to fit it into the kind of Chinese nationalism that the party wants,” says David Porter, a scholar of imperial China at McGill University in Montreal. “It’s easier to criticise Western historians for going the wrong way.”

The anti-Qing voices probably do not add up to anything significant for China’s contemporary politics. They are not about to coalesce into a movement that challenges party rule. They are discomfiting, not destabilising. They also underline how the space for public disagreements in China has narrowed. Other countries have plenty of historical controversies, too. China stands out for its inability to hold a full-throated debate about them. The party is too thin-skinned for that.

For their part, nationalists are guilty of over-simplifying Chinese history. Romanticising pre-Qing epochs as pure expressions of Han strength omits that China was a multi-ethnic, even cosmopolitan, entity during one of its most glorious periods, under the Tang dynasty more than a millennium ago. An honest accounting of this record would argue for China’s leaders today to be more tolerant and open, and to be confident of what such permissiveness would yield. Just do not hold your breath. ■

item.title: Donald Trump is shifting America’s military footprint
item.description:
United States

United States | Imperfect posture IN HIS BOOK “Strategy of Denial”, published in 2021, Elbridge Colby argued that America’s armed forces were too stretched to deal with every enemy around the world. Mr Colby, then a think-tanker who had served in Donald Trump’s first administration, declared t...
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump is shifting America’s military footprint

United States | Imperfect posture


IN HIS BOOK “Strategy of Denial”, published in 2021, Elbridge Colby argued that America’s armed forces were too stretched to deal with every enemy around the world. Mr Colby, then a think-tanker who had served in Donald Trump’s first administration, declared that China was the priority. America “should seek to avoid, reduce, or eliminate costly or demanding commitments in other parts of the world”, he maintained. “What is used for the Middle East”, he predicted, “will not be available for Asia.” That analysis is holding up, perhaps to Mr Colby’s dismay.

For more than 80 years America built a military footprint to assert itself as global policeman. Now Donald Trump is redefining America’s role, with Mr Colby as the Pentagon’s policy chief. In his national defence strategy, published in January, Mr Trump criticised previous administrations that had fought “war after rudderless war” and promised a “focused” approach.

In the Middle East, though, America is not only failing to prune forces, but waging a war with Iran that has recently escalated, with four American soldiers killed in recent days and more than 100 injured since July 7th. Cuts in Europe have so far been limited and done little to bolster defences in the Pacific. Far from gaining new focus, under Mr Trump, America’s military presence remains stubbornly diffuse.

Start with Europe, which has seen the most drastic change. Mr Trump has already withdrawn two of the five brigade combat teams, each around 4,000 troops, that were sent to Europe after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Confusingly, he has said he would send an “additional” 5,000 troops to Poland, but these are likely to come from elsewhere in Europe. More important, in June the Department of War (DoW) said it was reducing by a third forces earmarked for NATO in wartime, including fighter jets, destroyers and submarines.

Further cuts may come. In June, Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, announced a six-month review of America’s soldiers and military bases in Europe. “It will be designed to ensure that NATO is moving fast and irreversibly toward Europe leading, stepping up to take primary responsibility for the defence of Europe,” he said in Brussels. The administration favours fewer American resources in Europe, but more use of European ones—Mr Hegseth suggested that America would demand more unfettered access to European airspace and bases, some of which allies placed off-limits for the war against Iran.

How aggressively Mr Trump advances these plans depends, unusually, on Congress. The body has shown rare resistance to the president through its reauthorisation of defence spending. In December it imposed barriers to keep the president from shrinking American forces in Europe below 76,000 troops, only a few thousand short of the current level.

If progress in Europe is slower than Mr Trump would like, the hoped-for shift from the Middle East is heading in the wrong direction. America has removed all troops from Syria and will withdraw from Iraq in September. However, the war in Iran has diverted aircraft-carriers and air-defence systems, while depleting American munitions earmarked for a potential conflict with China. Around 50,000 troops are in the region, up from 40,000 before the war.

In the memorandum of understanding signed with Iran in June, America promised that it would remove forces from the “proximity” of Iran within 30 days. That now looks implausible. With its bases in the Gulf states battered by Iranian missiles, America has been running operations from more distant launchpads in Israel and Jordan. The question, whenever the war ends, is not whether America will dramatically shrink its presence in the Middle East, but what that presence will look like. Officials in Tel Aviv speak of shifting bases to Israel, where America has just one permanent deployment. But any hint of abandoning the Gulf, where leaders have cultivated close ties with Mr Trump, would be diplomatically explosive.

Whether the Americas also become a drag on resources depends on the president’s ambitions there. His national security strategy, published last year, identified the security of American soil and the wider western hemisphere as the priority. Mr Trump has already toppled one local leader, Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela, and is considering military options against Cuba. That would pull America’s stretched navy back to the Caribbean. Even more activity may follow. Recent investment in infrastructure in places such as Puerto Rico and Trinidad and Tobago suggests permanent deployments, says Jennifer Kavanagh of Defence Priorities, a think-tank.

From their vantage point in the Pacific, American admirals observe these developments—none of which does much to help them. America’s military posture in Asia has not been entirely static. In Guam, an American island 2,700km east of Taiwan, a buildup is causing housing costs to rise. Australia is upgrading a submarine base at Perth, on its west coast, which will allow American subs to stay in the region for longer. American marines have brought more potent missiles to the Philippines. Across the region, airfields are being improved and exercises are getting larger.

Nevertheless, the quantity of American troops and hardware in the Pacific has remained steady. For much of this year, America has deployed just one carrier in Asia, rather than the preferred two, the longest such gap for five years. America has 55,000-odd troops in Japan and around half that in South Korea.

The biggest changes amount to reshuffling within the region. In a speech in Seoul in January, Mr Colby praised South Korea as a “model ally” but raised eyebrows by failing to mention its main foe, North Korea. The Pentagon has toyed with the idea of withdrawing the most potent American unit, a 4,500-strong Stryker brigade, from the Korean peninsula, to focus it on China.

A huge influx of money would ease these dilemmas. Mr Trump has asked Congress for $1.5trn for the 2026-27 defence budget, a 44% rise. Even if that money were approved, it would not translate quickly into troops or equipment. Mr Colby, who once warned that America could not afford to wage multiple wars while still deterring China, now finds himself forced to craft a policy to do just that. ■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

item.title: The Iran war is America’s least popular since polls began
item.description:
United States

United States | No exit NEAR Martin Luther King’s stone memorial in Washington is a big golden cup honouring Donald Trump. The “Iran War Participation Trophy”, erected by anonymous satirists, suggests that on the battlefield it is not the winning that counts but the taking part. “While some con...
item.content:encoded:
The Iran war is America’s least popular since polls began

United States | No exit


NEAR Martin Luther King’s stone memorial in Washington is a big golden cup honouring Donald Trump. The “Iran War Participation Trophy”, erected by anonymous satirists, suggests that on the battlefield it is not the winning that counts but the taking part. “While some concern themselves with…measurable outcomes, President Trump demonstrated the courage to participate,” reads the inscription.

Maura Flint, a tour guide, says the joke is “very funny” but Mr Trump’s long war in Iran is anything but. “He doesn’t have a good strategy for getting out,” she complains. “There’s no end in sight.”

American voters seem to agree. As the ceasefire unravels, four-fifths think the war will last for “an extended period”, finds a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Nearly half think it will grind on for a year or more, according to Economist/YouGov polling. Few find the prospect appealing. Net approval for Mr Trump’s decision to attack Iran now stands at -30% among Americans. The war in Vietnam took six years to become as reviled as the Iran war has become in six months.

“The war with Iran is the most unpopular conflict among Americans since polls have been taken,” says Larry Sabato of the University of Virginia. The longer it goes on, “the more costs will mount, and one of those costs will be support for Trump and the GOP in the midterm elections.”

Public support for wars of choice often starts high but gradually falls. When America attacked Afghanistan in 2001, nearly 90% of Americans were in favour. President George W. Bush had offered a clear justification—the Taliban were sheltering the terrorists who had flown planes into New York skyscrapers. According to Gallup, it took 13 years for support to dip below 50%, by which time more than 2,000 Americans had been killed.

Far fewer Americans have died in Mr Trump’s war: 18 to date. But it has hit wallets in a way that is easy for voters to understand. Before Mr Trump attacked Iran, the Strait of Hormuz was open. Now it is not. After strenuous efforts to break Iran’s chokehold, Mr Trump claimed that “Oil is flowing like never before.” The pedants who measure such things beg to differ. Petrol now costs over $4 a gallon in America, up from $3 before the war.

The Vietnam war, which involved 3m American ground troops, quickly became what voters saw as America’s “most important problem”, according to Gallup. They do not say that about the Iran war. But they do tell pollsters that the issues they care most about include the “high cost of living” and “poor leadership”. So the Iran war could sway a lot of votes despite the relatively modest cost in American blood.

Among Democrats, net approval of the war is -84%. Among independents, it is -52%. The only large group that still backs it is MAGA Republicans, with a 72% net approval, and even this Trump-loving group is wavering. An Ipsos poll finds that, for the first time, significantly more than half of Trump supporters approve only “somewhat” of the way he is handling his job, rather than “strongly”. Republicans who call themselves “non-MAGA” have soured dramatically on the war, with net approval falling from +26% in April to -25% now.

On July 21st Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, begged Congress to authorise another $67bn in military spending. Democrats are reluctant, despite reports that funds are running short. Many accuse the administration of failing to account properly for the war’s cost. The Pentagon cites a figure of $37.5bn—largely the expense of spent munitions and fuel. Adding the costs of repairs to American bases and harm to consumers, Elissa Slotkin, a senator from Michigan, estimates it is more than five times that. She adds that Mr Trump’s sons are benefiting from Pentagon contracts.

The Economist’s midterms model gives Democrats an 81% chance of taking the House, and a 45% chance of flipping the Senate. Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment, a think-tank, says Mr Trump’s problems with Iran remind him of what Lyndon Johnson said about Vietnam: “I feel like a hitchhiker caught in a hailstorm on a Texas highway. I can’t run. I can’t hide. I can’t make it stop.” ■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

item.content:encoded:
美国右翼是如何开始憎恨共情的

美国 | 列克星敦

在美国右翼所鄙视的左翼诸多品质中，共情是最令人费解的一项。天哪，他们真是恨透了它。近年来，除了播客和社交媒体上无休止的讨论，还有一系列书籍将其视为——没错——一种罪过。2025年，乔·里格尼的《领导力与共情之罪》紧随前一年阿莉·贝丝·斯塔基的畅销书《有毒共情》之后出版。今年五月，营销学教授兼播客主加德·萨阿德的《自杀式共情》一经推出便迅速成为持续畅销书。萨阿德先生的销量无疑得益于封面上的埃隆·马斯克的推荐语，后者警告说：“西方文明注定要灭亡”，除非萨阿德的信息得到重视，并“采取艰难但必要的生存行动”。前共和党总统乔治·W·布什曾自称“富有同情心的保守派”，但这并非这种对共情的恐惧令人费解的原因；谴责共情是当今共和党人抹去他存在的又一种方式。它令人费解，是因为过度理解他人需求似乎很难解释民主党支持率惨淡的原因，即便唐纳德·特朗普通过中饱私囊、粉饰华盛顿以及毫无战略地发动战争疏远了大多数美国人。事实上，多年来一直有观点认为——列克星敦也曾试图论证——左翼的问题在于缺乏共情：对那些因技术和贸易而流离失所的美国人；对那些易受犯罪侵害的人；对那些因边境混乱而惊慌的人；对那些没有大学学历的人；对那些因税收高昂却换来糟糕政府服务而沮丧的人；对那些担心乔·拜登年事已高无法连任的人；以及对所有支持特朗普的人。说到共情，如果说有谁在“自杀”，那便是民主党。无论如何，当下西方世界似乎并不太担心共情过盛。然而萨阿德先生却担心“西方在无限宽容与狂欢式共情的祭坛上走向死亡”。作为一名犹太人，他在1975年黎巴嫩内战爆发时随家人逃离黎巴嫩前往加拿大，他对穆斯林移民的宽容尤为警惕。但他也在从新冠防疫措施到蒙特利尔“无尽自行车道”（所谓“基于气候的狂欢式情感失禁”的产物）等一切事物中看到了自杀式共情的证据（是的，“狂欢式”似乎是他最喜欢的词，耐人寻味）。亨特·拜登的笔记本电脑与自杀式共情有何关联尚不清楚。但萨阿德先生还是把它塞了进去，连同语言管控、纵容罪犯以及诸如“将恋童癖人性化以减少污名”之类的学术论文。在嘲讽“共情式收入平等”的同时，萨阿德先生对一位缺乏共情的受害者却流露出真正的温情。“每当我在社交媒体上发泄对纳税金额的不满时，很多人丝毫不同情我，”他抱怨道，“他们对我‘发牢骚’感到震惊。”事实上，萨阿德先生喜欢共情——只要它施予正确的人。作为一名进化心理学研究者，他主张自然选择使人类倾向于将共情指向最亲近的人。他这一点说得没错。在狩猎采集时代，共情帮助人类区分敌友、加强部落内部纽带。为强化这种机制，人类发展出一些认知偏见，包括“归因错误”——这促使他们原谅盟友的坏事，将其归因于环境，而将敌人的坏事视为低劣品格的证据。萨阿德先生就表现出这种偏见：他写道，大规模驱逐计划中出现“个别错误驱逐案例”是“统计上可预期的”。但他对非法移民所犯罪行却没有给予类似的统计赦免，含蓄地以一概全地抹黑所有人。他也没有谴责共和党领袖对反犹播客主或白人至上主义抗议者表现出的共情。与他对共情的看法一致，并且利于书籍销售，萨阿德先生选择了自己的部落。他所拥抱的共情形式，与他所谴责的左翼共情形式一样，都是加剧两极分化的强大引擎。随着信息技术的发展——从萨阿德先生这样的纸质书到马斯克拥有的X平台——人类已证明擅长利用其增强共情的部落化力量。问题在于，如今人们已不再生活在狩猎采集社会。当美国人和伊朗人之间相互理解不足，以至于无法有效开战，更别提实现和平时，一种更广阔的共情观念理应出现：不是“我感受到你的痛苦”的情感共情，而是认知共情，或心理学家所谓的“心智理论”——推断他人如何看待世界的能力。这是进化心理学研究者罗伯特·赖特另一本新书《上帝测试》的核心主题。审视人工智能的迅猛发展，赖特先生（列克星敦的前同事）警告说，作为朋友和顾问的谄媚AI代理可能极具部落化效应。此外，在令人信服地论证某种超级智能可能在十年内到来时，赖特先生认为，人类物种的生存现在可能取决于它能否克服公司、政党与国家之间的竞争本能。它们必须找到合作方式，建立护栏，防止潜在灾难，并实现人工智能的潜在福祉。“人工智能革命要求人类理解的革命：人类对人类的相互理解，”他写道。他寄希望于共同威胁能团结人类，但担心“我们物种所处的位置与它需要达到的位置之间的差距，几乎大到可笑。”这一点，我们确实能够共情。■

item.title: 挥之不去的关税
item.description:
United States

美国 | 层层加税 唐纳德·特朗普的关税如同九头蛇般顽固。最高法院在二月推翻了其主要的法律依据，焦虑的市场迫使多次让步，沮丧的选民——其中三分之二认为关税抬高了消费品价格——促使对某些食品实施豁免。每一次挫折都迫使特朗普调整关税。然而它们总是卷土重来。如今，美国的关税体系正通过一系列旧法规被重新激活。7月15日，政府依据《1974年贸易法》第301条，对部分巴西商品征收25%的关税。其列举的罪名包括偏袒本土支付系统、非法砍伐森林等。巧合的是，这一行动恰逢与巴西总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦的更大范围争端。 五天后，特朗普援引1930年《斯穆特-霍利关税法》中一项沉睡已久的条款，对部分...
item.content:encoded:
挥之不去的关税

美国 | 层层加税 唐纳德·特朗普的关税如同九头蛇般顽固。最高法院在二月推翻了其主要的法律依据，焦虑的市场迫使多次让步，沮丧的选民——其中三分之二认为关税抬高了消费品价格——促使对某些食品实施豁免。每一次挫折都迫使特朗普调整关税。然而它们总是卷土重来。如今，美国的关税体系正通过一系列旧法规被重新激活。7月15日，政府依据《1974年贸易法》第301条，对部分巴西商品征收25%的关税。其列举的罪名包括偏袒本土支付系统、非法砍伐森林等。巧合的是，这一行动恰逢与巴西总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦的更大范围争端。 五天后，特朗普援引1930年《斯穆特-霍利关税法》中一项沉睡已久的条款，对部分加拿大商品征收50%的关税，表面上是惩罚其邻国在汽车、酒精和乳制品上歧视美国。这些关税将覆盖近200亿美元的进口商品，包括通常根据《美墨加协定》（USMCA）享受豁免的商品——该协定由特朗普在其第一任期内谈判达成。然而新关税要到8月19日才生效——这一延迟将增强总统在停滞的USMCA续约谈判中的筹码。在这些战术性交锋背后是一个更大的计划：复活特朗普去年在“解放日”宣布的关税。对全部进口商品征收10%的关税以及针对特定国家的关税，均依据《1977年国际紧急经济权力法》实施——特朗普声称美国的贸易逆差构成国家紧急状态。在最高法院于二月否决后，政府依据《1974年贸易法》第122条征收了临时性10%附加费；该附加费将于7月24日到期。根据宾夕法尼亚沃顿预算模型，美国的平均有效关税税率已从法院裁决前的10%降至目前的7%。这些关税现在可能分两步复活。首先，美国贸易代表办公室预计将很快依据第301条，对60个被指控未能阻止使用强迫劳动生产的商品的国家征收强迫劳动关税。有利的是，这种对劳工标准的新关注将使特朗普在第122条附加费到期后仍能维持10%的关税。这些变化共同将使有效关税税率保持在目前约7%的水平。但它们可能很快进一步上升。今年晚些时候，美国贸易代表办公室预计将依据第301条对16个美国最大贸易伙伴的“结构性产能过剩”进行调查，并征收进一步的国别关税。政府指责这些国家“生产了超过其国内消费或生产性投资能力的商品”，智库进步政策研究所的埃德·格雷瑟称这一定义“古怪”。尽管借口可能牵强，但这些关税很可能持久。第301条赋予美国贸易代表办公室广泛的自由裁量权，以报复其认为不合理或歧视性的外国做法。法院“倾向于询问美国贸易代表办公室是否遵循了必要程序，”律师事务所King & Spalding的瑞安·马杰鲁斯表示，“而不是巴西是否真的存在森林砍伐问题。” 如果关税复活，它们会有效吗？关税已带来收入，并让特朗普能够同时施压盟友和敌人。但最具政治影响力的目标是他十年来促进制造业的承诺。供应管理研究所对采购经理的调查显示，工厂活动已连续六个月扩张。第二季度制造业产出年化增长率为4.6%，为2021年以来最快增速。财政部长斯科特·贝森特宣称美国正在“经历制造业复兴”。然而几乎没有证据表明关税正在推动工业复兴。近期几乎所有增长都来自先进制造业，主要源于人工智能相关需求。该行业其他领域停滞不前，工厂建设支出已从2024年近2500亿美元的年化峰值下降至5月的1750亿美元，降幅近三分之一。许多新增产能反映了特朗普再次当选前的投资。自他重返白宫以来，制造业就业岗位减少了约7.5万个。关税的成本也日益清晰。不确定性正在拖累投资：会计师事务所毕马威调查的商业领袖中，有一半表示对执行投资计划信心不足。根据哈佛商学院定价实验室的数据，关税已使消费者价格上升约0.8%，并可能进一步推高。纽约联邦储备银行的研究发现，近一半支付关税的企业仍预计将更多成本转嫁给客户。特朗普的关税或许能挺过法院。但它们能否挺过对价格敏感的选民，则不那么确定。■ 关注美国政治动态，请订阅我们的每日简报《美国速览》，快速分析最重要政治新闻；以及每周专栏《制衡》，审视美国民主状况及选民关注的问题。

item.title: The faltering effort to revive copper mining in Michigan
item.description:
United States

item.content:encoded:
The faltering effort to revive copper mining in Michigan

United States | Digging divides


Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, known as the UP, touches three of America’s Great Lakes. Wolves and moose roam the region’s forests; it is home to more than 80% of Michigan’s bears and less than 3% of its people. Nicknamed “Yoopers”, so many residents claim Finnish origin that, until 2015, local TV programming included a show in Finnish. In summer anglers fish for walleye and smallmouth bass. In winter the UP can get nine metres of snow. But this remote peninsula also has a belt of native copper and was once home to a thriving mining industry. If proponents have their way, the UP will become part of a 21st-century boom.

The Trump administration wants to promote mining in America, particularly of what it considers critical minerals, including copper. Proposed projects across the country would, if developed, remake swathes of American landscape, create jobs and reduce dependence on imports. In the UP the proposed Copperwood mine is, on paper, all but ready to go. However, it has been like that for years, and construction has not yet started. The gap between Made in America ambition and operating a mine can be as wide as a tailings site.

Developing a mine in America has long been an onerous process, with extensive environmental reviews and permitting requirements, as well as frequent litigation. Even if a project wins regulatory approval, margins are pinched by high costs of labour and construction. But recently anxiety about imports and a zeal for resource nationalism have coincided with booming demand for copper. Prices have risen by 60% in the past three years, as firms seek to expand power grids and build data centres.

American copper production could more than double to 2.5m tonnes a year, according to a recent study by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. That would all but cover what America now imports, mostly from Chile. The biggest opportunities are in Arizona and Alaska, rather than Michigan. But the Copperwood project, proposed by Highland Copper, is among the most advanced in the country, and almost fully permitted. In theory it would transform the area.

In the 19th century immigrants came to the UP from all over the world to dig up not just copper but other metals by hand. Town names reflect this: there’s an Ironwood, a Copper Harbor and a Silver City. After the second world war, industrial mining employed thousands. These days, however, the region has more mining museums than working mines.

Some would love the industry to return. “My grandfather worked in the mines, my uncles worked in the mines,” says Dan Siirila, a local county commissioner. In the early 1970s his high-school class had 250 pupils; now it has around 35.

As he drives your correspondent around the proposed Copperwood mine, Mike Foley, the site manager, explains what it will take to build it. Gesturing from the vehicle, he points out the land that will become the mine’s biggest feature: the tailings disposal facility. After it is all crushed by enormous rollers, perhaps 6% of what comes out of the ground is trucked out to smelters. The other 94% is piled up at the facility. It will cover the equivalent of 350 football pitches, with an enormous plastic liner to catch contaminated run-off water. “It’s like a landfill where you put your garbage,” Mr Foley brightly declares.

Not everyone is thrilled by this prospect. Tom Grotewohl, who runs “Protect the Porkies”, a campaign against the mine, lives in a rough cabin in the Porcupine Mountains within spitting distance of the site. By his own admission he is a NIMBY and an “off-grid Luddite”. He fears the dam holding back the tailings from Lake Superior could break, threatening the biodiversity of the UP. Highland Copper says this is exceptionally unlikely, though it has happened elsewhere. Often a project’s promised jobs can overwhelm environmental concerns, but industrial mining is too efficient to employ many people and there is not enough ore to open additional mines. Mr Grotewohl’s campaign has attracted almost half a million signatures of support and drawn hundreds of protesters to Lansing, Michigan’s capital.

The main barrier to the mine, however, is financial. Copperwood’s ore is roughly 1.5% copper. The Democratic Republic of Congo’s copper mines generally have grades of 6% or more. Some state politicians in Michigan have pushed for a $50m grant to support the construction of a new road and other infrastructure, but that measure has stalled. Much now depends on the possibility of federal cash. Highland Copper hopes to secure a $250m loan from America’s Export-Import Bank, which expressed interest last year. That would represent the majority of the project’s required financing.

Barry O’Shea, Highland Copper’s chief executive, contends that at current prices the mine is viable even without that support. Yet he admits that construction will start by 2028 at the earliest, and production not until 2030. That is plenty of time for copper prices, which are volatile, to fall once more.

Investors may run out of patience. In contrast to Mr O’Shea’s optimism, the firm’s latest annual report warns of “significant doubt about the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern”. The Trump administration’s Export-Import Bank may come to Copperwood’s rescue, with taxpayers footing the bill. Without it, the imagined transformation of this remote peninsula is likely to remain just that. ■

item.title: South America is eradicating hunger
item.description:
The Americas

The Americas | Eat up The smell of grilled meat wafts through the shanty town of Guamá. Its riverside favelas are among Brazil’s poorest, but on a recent weekday residents cooked steak and shrimp on their porches. “Life isn’t easy,” says Alex Lima, a shopkeeper who sells coxinha pasties from hi...
item.content:encoded:
South America is eradicating hunger

The Americas | Eat up


The smell of grilled meat wafts through the shanty town of Guamá. Its riverside favelas are among Brazil’s poorest, but on a recent weekday residents cooked steak and shrimp on their porches. “Life isn’t easy,” says Alex Lima, a shopkeeper who sells coxinha pasties from his wooden house on stilts in the coffee-coloured water. Yet it is improving, fast.

The share of people who are hungry has been decreasing faster in South America than anywhere else in the world. It is down by one-third since 2020, according to a report published on July 21st by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO). Just 3.5% of people in the region consume insufficient calories, the lowest level recorded. Eliminating hunger by 2030 is one of the UN’s “sustainable development” goals. “If there is a region in the world that can potentially achieve that, it’s South America,” says Máximo Torero, the FAO’s chief economist.

The continent has been here before. Hunger plummeted in the 2000s as a commodity boom lifted economic growth, allowing left-wing leaders to splurge on social programmes. In Venezuela Hugo Chávez created state-subsidised supermarkets. Argentina’s Néstor and Cristina Kirchner funded comedores populares (soup kitchens). Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva expanded credit for small-scale family farmers. The splurging worked, but when commodity prices fell in 2014, triggering recessions across the region, food insecurity shot up and stayed there. The pandemic made things worse. As unemployment surged, it dragged swathes of the middle class into poverty and hunger.

Yet most countries have recovered. Brazil led the way. Lula, as the president is commonly known, made food security a priority when he returned to office in 2023. By 2025 Brazil had made it off the UN’s Hunger Map, which tracks countries where more than 2.5% of the population suffers from chronic hunger. Chile and oil-rich Guyana were also removed. Argentina is almost there at under 3%. Colombia and Paraguay are approaching at 4%, while Peru and crisis-battered Venezuela are making inroads near 5%. Even Ecuador and Bolivia have improved a tad, to 11% and 20% respectively. Only Suriname is moving in the wrong direction.

This decline rests on sturdier foundations. The first is macroeconomic stability. South America’s central banks are far more independent and adept at managing inflation than they were two decades ago. Its monetary officials were quick to lift interest rates aggressively during the pandemic, getting inflation under control faster than elsewhere. While covid-19 stimulus packages did swell public debt, subsequent governments have trimmed spending, too much of which can pump up inflation. President Javier Milei’s shock therapy has yielded Argentina’s first primary surplus since 2008. Conservatives in Bolivia, Chile and Ecuador are also cutting spending. Newly elected right-wingers in Peru and Colombia pledge to do the same.

This eases pressure on grocery bills. Monthly food-price inflation in Argentina has slowed from a peak of almost 30% in 2023—among the world’s worst rates—to under 2% in June, lower than wage growth. Bolivia’s annual rate was 33% in November, when a right-wing president, Rodrigo Paz, took office. It’s now running at around 13%. In Ecuador food inflation has turned negative while wages are stable. Alongside big oil reserves, fiscal discipline has buffered South America from the economic shock of the Iran war.

Yet groceries that become more affordable over time do little to help those too poor to buy enough food today. Social programmes are the other pillar of South America’s success in reducing hunger. Most famous is Brazil’s Bolsa Família, a cash-transfer programme which pays families a stipend if they vaccinate their children and send them to school. Lula has also raised Brazil’s minimum wage. “These are the core policies,” says José Graziano da Silva, a former boss of the FAO.

Such measures were standard in the 2000s, too. However, they have become more sophisticated, says Elisabetta Recine of Consea, the Brazilian government’s advisory council on food security. Bolsa Família has digitalised payments and linked them to social registries, reducing fraud and increasing flexibility (so that, for instance, it can now cover seasonal workers who dip in and out of poverty). Colombia is looking at scrapping conditions on cash transfers to the poorest, whose children may not have a school to attend. Chile’s version includes job training.

Cash-transfer schemes are wildly popular. Right-wing politicians have embraced them. While in office, Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro tripled the average stipend provided by Bolsa Família. Mr Milei doubled funding for food stamps after receiving criticism from the Catholic church. Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s populist right-wing president-elect, has vowed to shrink the state by 40%, yet claims, optimistically, that he will not touch social handouts. Chile’s arch-conservative president, José Antonio Kast, has needed to invoke the spectre of drug crime in an effort to slash benefits, proposing a “vandals registry” that blocks those with a criminal record from receiving benefits.

Serious challenges remain. The biggest is climate change. With rising temperatures, plant pests and crop failures have become more common. The coming year looks especially fraught. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, a US government agency, says the coming cycle of the El Niño weather pattern will be “very strong”. That is the highest of the five categories used to rank the phenomenon, used for only the third time since 1950. “It’s going to aggravate every food problem,” says Carolina Trivelli, a former government minister in Peru.

That makes it a bad moment to fine-tune welfare schemes. Yet change is needed. Many countries struggle to wean recipients off cash-transfer programmes. A study found one-fifth of children who in 2005 were covered by Bolsa Família were still covered as adults in 2024. What began as a relatively cheap and focused project in 2003 has ballooned. It now costs 1.5% of GDP and covers nearly a fifth of households. The current design is discouraging workers from joining the formal sector, according to a paper by Daniel Duque of the Getulio Vargas Foundation, a university in São Paulo. “There are more efficient ways to fight hunger,” he says.

Then there is diet. The shares of children who are overweight and adults who are obese have surged to record levels of close to 10% and 30% respectively, among the worst in the world. Adjusted for purchasing power, South America is the fourth most expensive place in the world to procure a healthy diet, after the Caribbean, North Africa and South-East Asia. Fruits and vegetables are surprisingly expensive for an area known for growing them. That is because farmland is largely dedicated to commodities. When greens are produced, bad roads and dodgy cold chains yank up costs. Cash-strapped consumers are more likely to reach for processed, calorie-dense products.

These are manageable problems. New technologies are helping farmers adapt to a changing climate. Policymakers in Bolivia, Brazil and Peru have quietly acknowledged that certain programmes need better targeting. Improved labelling of healthier food is gaining ground, as are sin taxes, says Juliana Tângari of Comida do Amanhã, a Brazilian think-tank. No food system is perfect. Yet outright hunger may soon have rumbled its last in South America. ■

item.title: Brazil’s much-loved payments system has drawn Donald Trump’s ire
item.description:
The Americas

The Americas | Another trade-war misstep THE MACHINERY which moves money around is rarely inspiring. It is remarkable then that Pix, Brazil’s digital-payments system, has become a source of national pride after being assaulted by Donald Trump. On July 15th the Trump administration imposed a 25%...
item.content:encoded:
Brazil’s much-loved payments system has drawn Donald Trump’s ire

The Americas | Another trade-war misstep


THE MACHINERY which moves money around is rarely inspiring. It is remarkable then that Pix, Brazil’s digital-payments system, has become a source of national pride after being assaulted by Donald Trump. On July 15th the Trump administration imposed a 25% tariff on a range of Brazilian imports after concluding a year-long trade investigation into what it called Brazil’s “unreasonable” practices.

Pix was prominent among the grievances. Launched by the Central Bank of Brazil in 2020, it is loved by consumers for making payments instant and free. It is now part of everyday life in Brazil. Around 170m people—80% of the population—use it, and it accounts for more than half of the country’s payment transactions.

Some of the administration’s complaints about Brazilian trade practices have merit. Brazil is no free-trader. But the case against Pix rests on two shaky assumptions: that it is a protectionist tool and that it has damaged American payment companies (particularly Visa and Mastercard). Neither is supported by evidence.

Take protectionism. The complaint accuses Brazil of putting American firms at a disadvantage, but Pix’s rules do not distinguish between domestic and foreign participants. Any financial institution licensed in Brazil and operating there—as Visa and Mastercard do—is free to connect to the network on the same terms. All banks, Brazilian or foreign, with more than 500,000 account-holders in the country are required to offer Pix to their customers. But there is no requirement for payment processors like Visa and Mastercard to sign up. They have done so voluntarily.

The Trump administration also complains that Brazil’s central bank both operates Pix and regulates it. The arrangement does raise legitimate questions about giving so much control over a payments system and the financial data it generates to a single institution. But those are concerns about concentration of power, not about discrimination against foreign firms. Governments build, own and regulate essential infrastructure routinely. There is nothing inherently discriminatory about applying the same model to payments, points out Monica de Bolle of the Peterson Institute for International Economics, a think-tank in Washington.

The second assumption—that Pix has harmed American payment companies—is also weak. It rests on a misunderstanding over why Pix was created, says Daniel Santos Kosinski, a professor of economics at the State University of Rio de Janeiro. Before Pix, existing services, including those offered by foreign firms, charged fees for electronic payments that poor Brazilians could not afford. Pix was built to change that. The central bank estimates that at least 70m people have entered the formal financial system since its launch.

Far from cannibalising other electronic payment methods, Pix has expanded the market. It has done so at the expense of cash and cheques, the use of which has plummeted. The number of cash withdrawals made every quarter has fallen by 46% since Pix was introduced (see chart).

That does not mean incumbents face no pressure. Pix has changed the economics of payments. Bernardo Guimarães of Getulio Vargas Foundation, a university in Rio de Janeiro, says this may eventually squeeze the profits of Visa and Mastercard—but through lower fees, not fewer transactions. Businesses in Brazil typically pay around 2% of credit-card sales to a payment processor. A Pix payment costs next to nothing. The result is greater pressure on all payment processors, big and small, to justify the fees they charge.

The Trump administration’s deeper concern may be that Pix becomes a model for the rest of Latin America, eroding American card networks’ profits and their influence across the region. But that, too, is misguided. Pix was the product of Brazil’s particular circumstances: a powerful and trusted central bank that could require big banks to join the system, and a huge domestic market in which millions of people still relied on cash. It also took years to design and test. Few if any countries in Latin America have the same conditions.

The biggest beneficiary of Mr Trump’s campaign against Pix may well be Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, known as Lula. His political fortunes have improved ahead of a presidential election in October, thanks to his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro’s connection to a vast fraud scandal. America’s assault on Pix is another electoral gift. In a country riven by polarisation, the system is one of very few entities that enjoys broad support. Mr Trump’s campaign against it has allowed Lula to cast himself as the defender of one of Brazil’s most successful public innovations and, by extension, of sovereignty.

That leaves Mr Bolsonaro in an awkward position. His family’s close alliance with Mr Trump makes it tricky to defend Pix from his attacks. On July 2nd Mr Bolsonaro tried to find a workable line, suggesting to the Trump administration that Pix should be blocked from connecting to payment systems run by countries such as China and Russia. Lula immediately accused him of wanting to “hand over Pix to foreign interests”, and cast him as being more interested in pleasing America than defending Brazil. Memes mocking Mr Trump and Mr Bolsonaro proliferated. So far, all America’s campaign against Pix has achieved is to give Brazilians one more reason to love their payments system. ■

item.title: Nicaragua’s President Daniel Ortega scraps elections
item.description:
The Americas

The Americas | Leaders for life Given Donald Trump’s campaign against Cuba, imitating the place may seem unwise. Yet on July 19th Daniel Ortega, Nicaragua’s 80-year-old dictator, vowed to make his country only the second in Latin America to renounce competitive elections. Opposition parties wil...
item.content:encoded:
Nicaragua’s President Daniel Ortega scraps elections

The Americas | Leaders for life


Given Donald Trump’s campaign against Cuba, imitating the place may seem unwise. Yet on July 19th Daniel Ortega, Nicaragua’s 80-year-old dictator, vowed to make his country only the second in Latin America to renounce competitive elections. Opposition parties will “never again” be able to seek power through the ballot box, he declared. The former Marxist-Leninist guerrilla ruled from 1979 to 1990, then was elected president in 2006.

He may have misspoken. His political party has been trying to find friendly outfits to dress up as an opposition, says Félix Maradiaga, a former presidential candidate now in exile. But it is more likely that Mr Ortega is moving towards a formal one-party state.

Elections have long been a sham. In the most recent, in 2021, Mr Ortega jailed seven rival candidates. The Organisation of American States declared that the poll was “not free, fair or transparent”. He founded a dynasty in plain sight, having his wife, Rosario Murillo, appointed to the newly created office of co-president, poised to take his place when he can no longer act. He may like one of his five sons to follow.

The new rhetoric still matters: it is a “qualitative leap”, says Claudia Vargas, an exile whose husband was assassinated outside their home in Costa Rica last year. Will there be consequences for overtly dismantling democracy? The United States could impose them. On July 21st Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, asked the “international community” to “demonstrate to the Murillo-Ortega dictatorship that it cannot expect to maintain business as usual with other nations when it is thwarting the basic tenets of our democratic hemisphere”. With Venezuela now moulded to Mr Rubio’s liking and Cuba under pressure, Nicaragua would be an obvious next step.

Yet Mr Ortega may yet get away with it. Mr Trump has no problem making nice with dictators when it suits him. He is a fan of El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, whose legislature scrapped term limits last year. On July 13th Mr Bukele’s party confirmed him, unopposed, as its candidate for the election due in February 2027. ■

item.title: Gulf countries are experts at air-conditioning
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

Middle East & Africa | Keeping cool in the desert Back in the 1970s Gulf countries bet big on the idea that technology could make hot, arid places habitable. The gamble paid off. Abundant oil and gas fuelled construction, accelerated investment and powered round-the-clock cooling. The popul...
item.content:encoded:
Gulf countries are experts at air-conditioning

Middle East & Africa | Keeping cool in the desert


Back in the 1970s Gulf countries bet big on the idea that technology could make hot, arid places habitable. The gamble paid off. Abundant oil and gas fuelled construction, accelerated investment and powered round-the-clock cooling. The population of the Gulf Co-operation Council (GCC), a club of six petro-monarchies, grew from 6.3m in 1970 to 63m today.

That growth came at a cost. Air-conditioning units in flats and building-wide systems to keep the heat out of whole blocks gobble up power and produce emissions that accelerate warming. Today cooling accounts for as much as two-thirds of peak electricity demand in the GCC. So Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar have sought systems that would keep their cities liveable while using less power and doing less damage to the climate. As global warming makes air-conditioning necessary in ever more places, they want to export that technology to the rest of the world.

In some Gulf cities as much as a quarter of cool air comes from district-cooling systems. A central plant chills water and pumps it through a network of buildings. Energy use is reduced by sharing peak loads across the network. The system uses some 30% less power than in-building systems, and up to 80% less than if all flats in the district were cooled by individual air-conditioning units. The central plant also acts as a sort of battery. Chilled water is stored in tanks for use during periods of high demand.

Other countries, including Singapore and America, have similar systems, but few match the scale and design for extreme conditions seen in the Gulf. Tabreed, an Emirati firm, runs the world’s largest scheme in downtown Dubai, where it cools 80 buildings, including the Burj Khalifa and Dubai Mall. The company claims that, compared with older cooling methods, it reduces annual carbon emissions by about as much as removing 40,000 cars from the roads every year. It also runs what it calls a “zero waste” district-cooling system in Masdar City, Abu Dhabi, where geothermal energy powers the chillers and heat is pumped back into the ground.

District cooling requires copious water, a challenge in water-scarce regions such as the Gulf and many other places where air-conditioning demand will almost certainly grow. Gulf countries have cut freshwater usage by running the systems on treated waste water, rather than the potable sort. A plant in Saudi Arabia is using seawater. More recently, the countries have been looking to integrate cooling-hungry data centres for artificial intelligence (AI) applications into district-cooling systems. Tabreed is also experimenting with adding tiny particles to cooling water, letting it absorb more heat.

As the world warms and AI use expands, the need for such technologies will grow beyond the Gulf. Global demand for cooling could triple by 2050, according to one estimate used by the UN. The market for district cooling alone may roughly double to $60bn by 2034, according to another projection. Gulf companies are gearing up to be part of the expected bonanza. In India, where cooling demand may rise eightfold in the next decade, Tabreed is developing what it says will be Asia’s largest district-cooling system in the southern tech hub of Hyderabad. It is also breaking ground on projects in Egypt.

Though they are about 40% cheaper in the long term than other solutions, big-ticket systems remain expensive to build. GCC countries were rich enough for that; many other places may not be. Rich European countries could afford it, but have yet to reach political consensus on how much to invest in cooling and where to buy the tech. As extreme heat becomes more common, they will probably fork out the cash. Tabreed and other companies in the Gulf will be hoping to get a chunk of it. ■

item.title: How African motorists are adapting to the fuel crunch
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

Middle East & Africa | Power up Ethiopia trades in superlatives. It has Africa’s largest dam, is building its largest airport and claims to be the continent’s breadbasket (scepticism abounds). According to its transport ministry, the country has recently added another crowning achievement: ...
item.content:encoded:
How African motorists are adapting to the fuel crunch

Middle East & Africa | Power up


Ethiopia trades in superlatives. It has Africa’s largest dam, is building its largest airport and claims to be the continent’s breadbasket (scepticism abounds). According to its transport ministry, the country has recently added another crowning achievement: following an (unevenly enforced) import ban on vehicles with internal-combustion engines in 2024, it is now the leader of Africa’s electric-vehicle (EV) revolution. Some 115,000 EVs were zipping along its roads in 2025, says the ministry, accounting for nearly 8% of registered vehicles. If true, that would put it above the global average of around 5%.

The figures are almost certainly an overstatement. Experts balk at the transport ministry’s claim of 115,000 active EVs. Even other Ethiopian ministries estimate there were only 15,000 on the roads last year. That would still be an impressive feat for a country that had practically none a few years ago. But it is less an illustration of uniquely ambitious Ethiopian policy than a reflection of a continental trend. African motorists increasingly recognise that going electric can save them money. As the Iran war pushes up petrol prices and pinches pockets, many who can are making the switch.

Buying an EV saves money on fuel in the long run, but the upfront cost tends to be higher than that of a petrol-guzzling alternative. The higher the price of fuel, the more people will take the plunge. Ethiopia started phasing out a fiscally imprudent fuel subsidy in 2024, after entering an IMF programme. The ensuing rise in petrol prices persuaded many Ethiopians to buy EVs. But other Africans have also been going green. Sales of two- and three-wheel EVs on the continent grew by 38% in the year to May 2025, according to the Africa E-Mobility Alliance, a non-profit group. Sales of electric cars rose by 28%.

The Iran war has accelerated the trend. Yuma Sasaki, the founder of Dodai, an EV startup based in Ethiopia, reckons demand for his e-bikes is two or three times greater this year than last. Spiro, a Dubai-based firm that is Africa’s leading EV manufacturer, says it has more than 114,000 e-bikes on the road, an increase of 68% since December. BMI Research, a research firm, predicts that 8,300 EVs will be sold in South Africa this year, more than twice as many as in 2025, but still a small share of the 400,000 or so cars sold there annually.

Rising demand is driving investment. In Ethiopia Dodai is building two battery-swapping stations, where riders can switch empty batteries for fully charged ones, every month. Spiro recently raised $270m in fresh capital, valuing it at close to $1bn. It is also building a network of stations, particularly in east Africa. In most countries EVs are currently usable only in big cities, where charging or battery-swapping are available. But the infrastructure is expanding. Gagan Gupta, Spiro’s founder, claims that by next summer it will be possible to travel from Kenya through Uganda to Rwanda on one of his e-bikes.

Spiro also plans to build four big “mother plants” in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya and Nigeria to manufacture many of the components of its e-bikes, which can then be assembled in smaller facilities across the continent. The firm expects to buy some $400m-worth of batteries this year, rising to nearly $1bn-worth in 2027. It hopes to entice battery manufacturers to set up factories in Africa to supply its plants. “Because of our size and scale, we are able to push manufacturing closer to the continent,” Mr Gupta says, adding that this could lower production costs further.

Potholes lie ahead. Only two-wheeled EVs seem likely to scale up in Africa in the near future. Electric cars remain prohibitively expensive for most drivers, and charging stations suitable for them are much costlier to build than those that serve e-bikes. Vast improvements to Africa’s shoddy power grids will also be required so that charging stations function.

Yet African governments have every reason to speed things along. Building the infrastructure necessary for EVs would mean less-polluted cities and more reliable power for citizens. It could also save cash-strapped treasuries billions of dollars on fuel imports. Africa’s EV revolution cannot move fast enough. ■

Sign up to the Analysing Africa, a weekly newsletter that keeps you in the loop about the world’s youngest—and least understood—continent.

item.title: 非洲巨型项目的回归
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

中东与非洲 | 宏伟构想 多年来，肯尼亚北部海岸的拉穆一直是未兑现承诺的诱人象征。拉穆港-南苏丹-埃塞俄比亚-运输（LAPSSET）走廊是一个耗资预计250亿美元的庞大计划，旨在通过管道、铁路和高速公路，将肯尼亚的一个深水港与埃塞俄比亚的市场以及南苏丹的油田连接起来。该项目于2012年启动，曾被吹捧为非洲最雄心勃勃的基础设施工程。然而14年后，只有拉穆附近的港口在运营——而且自2021年首批船只停靠以来，大部分时间都只是勉强维持。“刚开始时非常冷清，”港口经理阿卜杜拉齐兹·姆泽承认。但现在，拉穆港正在从沉睡中苏醒，走廊的规划也被重新提上日程。直接原因是伊朗战争。自2月以来，数十艘原本驶往波斯...
item.content:encoded:
非洲巨型项目的回归

中东与非洲 | 宏伟构想 多年来，肯尼亚北部海岸的拉穆一直是未兑现承诺的诱人象征。拉穆港-南苏丹-埃塞俄比亚-运输（LAPSSET）走廊是一个耗资预计250亿美元的庞大计划，旨在通过管道、铁路和高速公路，将肯尼亚的一个深水港与埃塞俄比亚的市场以及南苏丹的油田连接起来。该项目于2012年启动，曾被吹捧为非洲最雄心勃勃的基础设施工程。然而14年后，只有拉穆附近的港口在运营——而且自2021年首批船只停靠以来，大部分时间都只是勉强维持。“刚开始时非常冷清，”港口经理阿卜杜拉齐兹·姆泽承认。但现在，拉穆港正在从沉睡中苏醒，走廊的规划也被重新提上日程。直接原因是伊朗战争。自2月以来，数十艘原本驶往波斯湾的船只已改道至拉穆相对安全的港口。然而，对LAPSSET的重新讨论也标志着非洲政策制定者和一些投资者思维更广泛的转变。非洲正在进入一个“巨型项目”的新时代，这些项目耗资数十亿美元，影响数百万人。问题是，这将加速增长，还是给这片大陆增添更多面子工程。 三个特定项目尤其说明了这股热潮。2025年，埃塞俄比亚完成了非洲最大的水电站——埃塞俄比亚复兴大坝（GERD）。一年前，尼日利亚实业家、非洲首富阿里科·丹格特在尼日利亚商业首都拉各斯附近启动了一座价值200亿美元的炼油厂。此外还有洛比托走廊，这是一个耗资数十亿美元的铁路、港口和公路系统，将连接安哥拉的大西洋海岸与刚果的铜矿带，并最终延伸至赞比亚（见地图）。该项目得到了美国和欧盟的支持。加纳智库Imani的布莱特·西蒙斯认为，非洲政策制定者的雄心“大幅提升”。1月，埃塞俄比亚破土动工了一座预计耗资至少125亿美元的新机场。尼日利亚正在重启一项长期搁置的计划，建设一条价值150亿美元的西非运输走廊。7月19日，西非领导人表示，一条从尼日利亚沿大西洋海岸延伸至摩洛哥、并可能连接欧洲天然气的价值250亿美元天然气管道，可能于2028年开工建设。泛非贷款机构非洲金融公司（AFC）表示，非洲的铁路建设正在加速，目前在建和开发中的铁路里程约7000公里，是2020年至2024年期间的两倍多。其中大部分是必要的。主要由富裕国家组成的经合组织（OECD）估计，到2040年使非洲GDP翻一番，非洲大陆每年需要在基础设施上投入1550亿美元（约占GDP的5.6%），这几乎是2016年至2020年年均水平的两倍，略低于中国在2010年代初的国内支出占比（GDP的6.7%）。然而，援助削减和债务正在挤压政府财政。2025年，非洲国家预计将支付890亿美元用于偿还债务。这还是在伊朗战争推高利率之前的情况（油价上涨缓解了石油出口国的影响，但进一步挤压了其他国家的财政）。因此，需要私人资本来填补缺口。2021年至2024年间，非洲所有行业每年筹集的私人资金总额从132亿美元稳步增长至204亿美元。总体而言，2025年非洲吸引了约700亿美元的外国直接投资，为1990年以来的第三高水平。私人基础设施发展集团的菲利普·瓦拉胡表示，去年是他专注于非洲和亚洲的捐赠支持基金自近25年前成立以来最好的一年。尽管全球危机不断，他补充说，今年“我们看到业务量仍在持续增长”。有几个理由可以预期这股推动力将持续下去。一是AFC的萨梅赫·谢努达所称的成功项目（如丹格特炼油厂）的“示范效应”。另一个是全球动荡，尤其是能源市场。能够减少对外部冲击脆弱性的基础设施显得更加紧迫。以拉穆为例。肯尼亚贷款机构股权银行老板詹姆斯·姆旺吉认为，LAPSSET“因中东危机而获得了顺风”。7月7日，丹格特先生表示他将在肯尼亚建造东非最大的炼油厂，这一决定因需要遏制该地区对从海湾进口燃料的依赖而被加速推进。据报道，拉穆港周边地区是他青睐的选址。中美之间的竞争也推动了大型基础设施投资。美国国际开发金融公司（DFC）以5.5亿美元支持洛比托走廊，希望将该地区关键矿产的出口从中国手中夺走。美国外交官也热切希望DFC投资于埃塞俄比亚的新机场，部分原因是为了帮助美国建筑公司领先于中国竞争对手。多边贷款机构的态度也发生了变化。在后独立时代，世界银行等机构曾支持非洲许多宏大的现代化项目，但在许多项目未能启动或陷入腐败丑闻后，它们退出了数十年。世界银行东非和南部非洲副总裁恩迪亚梅·迪奥普指出，如今“对大型项目的风险偏好”更高了。然而，大型项目仍具争议。关于土地使用和环境的斗争往往尤为激烈。7月7日，乌干达农民在伦敦提起法庭诉讼，要求阻止一条通往坦桑尼亚海岸的56亿美元输油管道，称其威胁水源和生态系统（该管道运营公司在英国注册）。此类项目也往往比宣传的延误更多、成本更高；据估计，约90%的项目超支。在非洲，这一风险可能更高，因为存在西蒙斯所称的“走廊溢价”：由基础设施严重匮乏带来的额外成本。他认为，单个项目要成功，首先必须建成一个集成的电力、道路等走廊。如果缺少一个环节，整个计划就可能崩溃。这并不意味着新项目注定失败。曾参与几内亚西芒杜矿业综合体的泛非工业集团Neemba的让-吕克·科南指出，交付基础设施“迫使你建立长期的国内能力”。因此，一个国家执行和维持大型项目的能力会随着时间的推移而增长。然而，仅靠雄心是永远不够的。■ 订阅《分析非洲》周刊，了解这个世界上最年轻、最不为人知的大陆的最新动态。

item.title: 为什么非洲年轻人仍然听广播
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

中东与非洲 | 调频收听 肯尼亚通信管理局正面临一个在数字时代看似奇怪的问题：内罗毕的无线电波已经拥堵不堪。肯尼亚拥有超过250家调频广播电台，还有众多正在申请中的新电台。在首都这样的大城市里，有志成为广播明星的人抱怨说，已经没有空间再发放更多许可证了。这一问题反映出广播在非洲出人意料的生命力。随着社交媒体和智能手机的普及，你可能会以为它们已经在注意力争夺战中胜出。然而，根据民调机构“非洲晴雨表”4月发布的一项调查，广播新闻在非洲大陆的影响力依然强劲。 广播塔最早于20世纪20年代在非洲各地竖立起来。殖民政权利用广播进行宣传。解放运动则设立秘密电台来组织抵抗。20世纪60年代，后殖民政府开始...
item.content:encoded:
为什么非洲年轻人仍然听广播

中东与非洲 | 调频收听

肯尼亚通信管理局正面临一个在数字时代看似奇怪的问题：内罗毕的无线电波已经拥堵不堪。肯尼亚拥有超过250家调频广播电台，还有众多正在申请中的新电台。在首都这样的大城市里，有志成为广播明星的人抱怨说，已经没有空间再发放更多许可证了。这一问题反映出广播在非洲出人意料的生命力。随着社交媒体和智能手机的普及，你可能会以为它们已经在注意力争夺战中胜出。然而，根据民调机构“非洲晴雨表”4月发布的一项调查，广播新闻在非洲大陆的影响力依然强劲。

广播塔最早于20世纪20年代在非洲各地竖立起来。殖民政权利用广播进行宣传。解放运动则设立秘密电台来组织抵抗。20世纪60年代，后殖民政府开始补贴晶体管收音机；国家控制的频率宣传着国家建设者宏大的现代主义梦想。有时它们也被用于更险恶的目的。在1994年卢旺达种族大屠杀前夕，一家与胡图族主导政权有关联的电台通过称图西族人为“蟑螂”来煽动仇恨。然而，大约在同一时期，非洲大陆的民主化浪潮迫使国家控制放松。商业电台如雨后春笋般涌现。

近年来，社交媒体激发了愤怒的年轻人抗议从肯尼亚到马达加斯加等国的政府。然而，根据“非洲晴雨表”的数据，城市和农村中仍有约60%的人每周多次收听广播新闻。即使是年轻人也是如此。约55%的18至35岁非洲人表示他们经常从广播中获取新闻，仅略低于将社交媒体列为主要信息来源的58%。

这种持久的吸引力如何解释？广播成本低廉且易于获取。即使是最便宜的手机也内置了调频收音机，且无需昂贵的移动数据即可收听。许多听众在非洲特大城市的交通堵塞中拨打电话参与节目。互联网非但没有损害广播，反而可能帮助了广播明星。知名主持人已成为社交媒体名人。在肯尼亚，一位主持人吹嘘说，他在广播成名后，如今大部分收入来自网上的品牌代言。

肯尼亚也在利用互联网解决频率短缺问题。继加纳和塞内加尔之后，它正在试验DAB广播，这种技术将无线电波压缩成数字数据，以便为更多电台腾出空间。■

订阅《分析非洲》周刊，了解这个世界上最年轻、也最不为人知的大陆的最新动态。

item.title: Lebanon’s president wants to enlist Donald Trump in rebuilding the country
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

Middle East & Africa | The Levant’s toughest knot In his office in downtown Beirut, Amer Bisat looks to the past to sketch a hopeful vision of the future. Lebanon was once the region’s premier entrepôt, a hub for banking, tourism and trade; perhaps it can be so again. “If reconstruction ev...
item.content:encoded:
